hindi: अर्जुन कहते हैं: “जो राजा लोग यहाँ युद्ध करने के लिए इकट्ठे हुए हैं और दुष्ट बुद्धि वाले दुर्योधन को खुश करना चाहते हैं, मैं उन्हें ध्यान से देखना चाहता हूँ।”
english: Arjuna says to Krishna, “I want to look at all those who have gathered here to fight. They have come to please the evil-minded son of Dhritarashtra by taking his side in this battle.”
deeper: Arjuna is still a calm, ready warrior. He does not rush in. He asks Krishna to stop the chariot so he can see clearly who is standing on the field. A wise person first understands the situation and only then acts.

Notice why Arjuna says these people have come: priya-chikīrṣavaḥ, “wishing to please.” Many of them are not there because they hate the Pandavas. They are there to keep Duryodhana happy. Arjuna’s eyes are noticing that people often join a side out of loyalty, habit or wanting to please someone, not because the cause is right.

This verse is also the quiet start of Arjuna’s great confusion. The more he looks at the faces on the field, the more his heart will be shaken. Looking carefully is good. But as the next verses show, a mind that looks while afraid or full of feeling can get overwhelmed. That is why Arjuna will soon need Krishna’s guidance.
words: those who are about to fight
I wish to look at, I want to see
of the evil-minded, of the one with bad judgment
background: The two great armies, the Pandavas and the Kauravas, stand facing each other on the field of Kurukshetra, ready for battle. The conch shells have been blown and the weapons are about to fly (1.20). Arjuna lifts his bow and speaks to his charioteer, Krishna.

He asks Krishna to drive the chariot to the middle, between the two armies (1.21), and to hold it there until he has carefully looked at the warriors who are ready and eager to fight (1.22). In this verse he explains what he wants to see: who exactly has come to side with Duryodhana.
lessons: Before a big action, stop for a moment and see the situation clearly.
Understanding who is involved and why they are there helps you judge wisely.
Many people take a side just to please someone, so do not follow others without thinking.
Joining a group only because everyone else is in it is not always a good reason.
Looking at a hard situation can stir big feelings, so keep a calm heart and seek good guidance.
examples: Before a gully cricket match, Aarav looks at who is playing on each side and why. He sees one friend has joined only because the captain gave him a chocolate.
Sana hears shouting in the corridor. Before taking sides, she asks what really happened instead of just joining the crowd.
Ravi sees many classmates teasing a new boy. He wonders, “Do they really want to do this, or are they just trying to please the leader of the group?”
Diya wants to rush into a quarrel with her cousin. She stops, takes a breath and looks at the whole picture first.
At a school election, Kabir looks around and sees which friends are backing a candidate out of real belief and which are just following the popular child.
Meera notices some children laugh at the bully’s jokes only because they want him to like them. She realises that is why the bullying keeps going.
Everyone in the group chat is saying something unkind about a classmate. Imran asks himself, “Am I agreeing only to fit in?”
Before choosing a club, Tara visits each one and watches who is there and what they do, instead of picking the one her friends picked.

story.title: Kabir and the Kabaddi Match
paras: In a small town in Punjab, Kabir’s school team was about to play a kabaddi match against the next street’s team. Their captain, Rohan, was loud and always wanted to win, even by tricks. Kabir noticed that Rohan wanted to secretly loosen the other team’s shoelaces before the game.

Before the match, Kabir asked the coach, “Please give me a minute to look around.” He walked slowly along his own team’s line and looked at each friend’s face. Some were nervous. Some looked unsure. A few whispered, “I don’t like this, but Rohan will be angry if I say no.”

Kabir understood something. Most of his team was not there to cheat. They were only trying to please Rohan. They were afraid of upsetting him. Kabir took a deep breath and said, “Friends, let us play fair and win by our own strength.” Slowly, one by one, the others nodded with relief.
Rohan was surprised, but he saw that nobody was following him anymore. The match was played fairly. Kabir’s team lost by two points, but everyone walked off the field with their heads high.
story.moral: Lesson: Look carefully at who is with you and why. Many people follow only to please someone, so think before you go along.

quiz.q: What does Arjuna want to do in this verse?
o: Look carefully at those who have come to fight
quiz.x: Arjuna wants to see clearly who has gathered on the battlefield.

quiz.q: Why does Arjuna say these warriors have come?
quiz.x: The word priya-chikīrṣavaḥ means “wishing to please.”
“Durbuddheḥ dhārtarāṣṭrasya” refers to Dhritarashtra’s son Duryodhana.

quiz.q: What is the main lesson for us?
o: Look carefully and think before taking a side
quiz.x: Arjuna pauses to see clearly, and we should too.

reel.hook: Why is everyone really standing on that side?
reel.lesson: Before you follow a group, look carefully at why people are there.
reel.caption:
Arjuna paused to see who had really come to fight, and why. 👀
Next time you feel pulled to join a crowd, stop and look first.
What do you notice? 🌟
